latest_nl_proof:
Let n be any natural number. Since g maps N to N and N = {1,2,3,...}, we have g(n) in N, hence g(n) >= 1. Therefore g(g(n)) is also a natural number, so g(g(n)) >= 1.

Because r >= 0, every real number x >= 1 satisfies x^r >= 1. Applying this with x = g(g(n)), we get
(g(g(n)))^r >= 1.
By the hypothesis,
g(n+1) - g(n) >= (g(g(n)))^r >= 1.
Thus for every n,
g(n+1) >= g(n) + 1 > g(n).
In particular, consecutive values of g are strictly increasing.

Now let m,n be natural numbers with m < n. Repeatedly using the inequality just proved, we obtain
g(m) < g(m+1) < g(m+2) < ... < g(n).
Hence g(m) < g(n). So g is strictly increasing.

The inequality g(n+1) >= g(n)+1 has already been established above for every n.

Finally, we prove g(n) >= n for all n by induction on n.
Base case: n = 1. Since g(1) is a natural number, g(1) >= 1.
Inductive step: assume g(n) >= n for some n. Then
g(n+1) >= g(n) + 1 >= n + 1.
So the claim holds for n+1.
By induction, g(n) >= n for every n in N.

Therefore g is strictly increasing, and consequently for every n in N we have g(n+1) >= g(n)+1 and g(n) >= n.
role_in_parent: Supplies the monotonicity and lower bound g(n) >= n needed before the upper-bound contradiction.
statement_nl: Let r be a real number with r \ge 0. Suppose g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} satisfies g(n+1)-g(n) \ge (g(g(n)))^r for every n \in \mathbb{N}. Then g is strictly increasing. Consequently, for every n \in \mathbb{N}, one has g(n+1) \ge g(n)+1 and g(n) \ge n.

domain_restrictions: r is a real number and r >= 0
g is a function from N to N (outputs are integers >= 0 unless N is taken to be positive integers); the intended argument requires outputs >= 1 to avoid 0^0 and to force RHS >= 1
N should be specified (common intended choice: N = {1,2,3,...}); if N contains 0 and g can take the value 0, special-cases arise
Exponentiation (g(g(n)))^r uses standard real exponentiation; the case base = 0 and r = 0 is indeterminate unless excluded
statement_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: Assume r ∈ R with r >= 0 and assume N denotes the positive integers (N = {1,2,...}) so that g: N -> N has values >= 1. If g satisfies ∀ n ∈ N, g(n+1) - g(n) >= (g(g(n)))^r, then for every n ∈ N, (1) g(n+1) - g(n) >= 1, hence g(n+1) >= g(n)+1 (so g is strictly increasing), and (2) by iteration g(n) >= g(1) + (n-1) >= n, so ∀ n ∈ N, g(n) >= n.
quantifier_order: Fix a function g: N -> N satisfying the hypothesis
Conclusion: ∀ n ∈ N, g(n+1) > g(n) (equivalently ∀ n, g(n+1) >= g(n)+1) and ∀ n, g(n) >= n

witness_dependencies: No existential witnesses are introduced by the statement: all quantifiers are universal (r fixed, g fixed, then ∀ n ...) so there are no dependent existential quantifiers
Consequential inequalities (g(n+1) >= g(n)+1 and g(n) >= n) follow uniformly from the hypothesis and do not require per-n existential choices
